🚀 Announcing Skilgen — open source. After spending the past few months thinking deeply about how AI coding agents actually work in practice, I kept coming back to one thing: 👉 It’s not just about agents 👉 It’s about the skills behind them Most of the time, we try to improve outputs with better prompts. But the real limitation is that agents lack structured, reusable understanding of your project. That’s exactly what Skilgen is built to solve. 🔗 https://lnkd.in/gdUXtGHc In the AI coding space, we’ve been focusing heavily on agents. But the real bottleneck I kept running into was this: 👉 Agents are only as good as the skills and context they operate with. Skilgen changes that. It turns your codebase and requirements into a living skills system for AI coding agents. Instead of manually crafting prompts or repeating context, it generates structured understanding and reusable skills like: --> FEATURES.md --> REPORT.md --> TRACEABILITY.md --> skills/MANIFEST.md --> domain-specific skills/**/SKILL.md So your agents don’t start from scratch every time, they operate with real project awareness. The result: <> More consistent, high-quality code output <> Alignment with enterprise-grade engineering standards <> Better architectural decisions (not just code generation) <> Reduced prompt engineering overhead <> Reusable knowledge across teams and projects <> Improved traceability between requirements and implementation <> Faster onboarding for new developers and agents <> Less “hallucination-driven” coding, more grounded execution And getting started is simple: !pip install skilgen This is my contribution to the open-source community, and I’m really curious how others think about this shift from prompts → skills. LangChain just changed the game by open-sourcing Deep Agents. For months, Claude Code has been the gold standard for terminal-based engineering, but it came with a catch: you were locked into one provider and one proprietary ecosystem. 🛠️ Why "Deep Agents" is a Production Game-Changer It’s a full-stack orchestration layer that brings the best of agentic reasoning to any model you choose (Claude, GPT-5, Gemini, or even local Llama instances). Here is what’s under the hood: Explicit Planning: The agent uses a write_todos tool to break down complex objectives before it touches your code. This transparency is the difference between a "hallucination loop" and a successful PR. Native Filesystem Access: Full navigation capabilities (read, write, grep, glob). It understands your directory structure as a human engineer would. Sandboxed Shell Execution: You can run builds, tests, and deployments directly from the agent in an isolated environment. Sub-Agent Delegation: This is the most critical feature for 2026. You can spawn isolated workers for sub-tasks, preventing the "context rot" that happens when a single agent tries to do too much at once. Context Management: It natively handles conversation compression and large output offloading—the "boring" parts of agent engineering that usually take weeks to get right. Deep Agents is built on LangGraph, which means you get all the enterprise-grade perks—streaming, persistence, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints—out of the box, but without the "Anthropic-only" handcuffs. pip install deepagents 📌 The Repo in comments Stay Data-Driven, Ilya hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #LangChain hashtag #DeepAgents hashtag #OpenSource hashtag #MLOps hashtag #SoftwareArchitecture hashtag #LangGraph hashtag #AIAgents hashtag #Python …more

🚀 LangChain just released Deep Agents and it might be the simplest way to build production-grade AI agents yet. I've been digging through the docs and the GitHub repo and here's what makes it genuinely interesting: What is it? Deep Agents is the easiest way to start building agents powered by LLMs, with built-in capabilities for task planning, file systems for context management, subagent-spawning, and long-term memory. Think of it as a fully wired agent "harness": you get a working agent in seconds, and customize only what you actually need. What's included out of the box: Planning via write_todos/read_todos for task breakdown, full filesystem access (read, write, edit, ls, glob, grep), shell execution with sandboxing support, sub-agents for delegating work with isolated context windows, and smart context management with auto-summarization when conversations get long. Why it stands out: The virtual filesystem is powered by pluggable backends, you can swap from in-memory state, local disk, LangGraph store for cross-thread persistence, or sandboxes like Modal, Daytona, or Deno for isolated code execution. It's 100% open source under MIT, fully provider-agnostic (Claude, OpenAI, Google, or any LangChain-compatible model), and built on LangGraph for production-ready streaming, persistence, and checkpointing. There's also a CLI tool for a terminal-based coding agent , pipe tasks, run interactively, teach it your preferences over time. 🚀 LangGraph 1.1 is out! This release is all about making LangGraph outputs type safe and easier to work with. Here's what's new: 1. Type-safe streaming — stream() now yields unified StreamPart typed dicts with consistent shape across every stream mode and subgraph depth, with full editor and type-checker narrowing. 2. Type-safe invoke — invoke() returns a GraphOutput object with typed output and interrupt access. 3. Pydantic and dataclass coercion — if your state/output schema is a Pydantic model or dataclass, outputs are automatically coerced to the right type. All fully opt-in, with no breaking changes. You don’t know what your agent will do until it’s in production. Agents are different from traditional software. Instead of defined paths and tests that can cover most major flows, agents take unbounded natural language input. That means even small prompt changes can cause big shifts in an agent’s behavior. They take unbounded natural language input, behave differently with small prompt changes, and make decisions across multi-step reasoning, retrieval, and tool calls. So when something goes wrong, it’s not enough to monitor latency, uptime, or error rates. You need to see: - what the user actually asked - how the agent reasoned - which tools it called - where it failed - and whether the outcome was actually useful This is why production monitoring for AI agents is fundamentally different from traditional observability. If you’re building agents, the real challenge isn’t just shipping them. It’s understanding what they do once real users start using them. Read more on what teams need to monitor in production, what breaks most often, and how leading companies are improving agent quality over time. https://lnkd.in/gdyhBD2E …more

Came across an interesting concept from Harrison Chase at LangChain that reframes the Agent stack. 💡 I’ve been reading up on the term "𝐀𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬," and the 𝐈𝐫𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐧 analogy helps make sense of where the industry might be heading. Here is the mental model: 🧠 The LLM is Tony Stark (raw intelligence). 🛠️ The 𝐅𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 (LangChain, LlamaIndex) is the Blueprint. You get the components: LLM wrappers, prompt templates, tool abstraction but you assemble everything yourself. To make the agent work, you have to build: • Tool invocation logic and routing • Memory and context management • Code execution sandbox • Error handling and retry logic • State persistence and checkpointing 🚀 The 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 ( hashtag #Claude Code SDK, DeepAgents) is the Assembled Suit. The infrastructure is built and running out of the box. The "boring" but critical systems are already active: • Code execution sandbox • File system operations (read/write with permissions) • Memory management (context window handling) • Error recovery (retry logic, state restoration) • State persistence (conversation history) 𝑾𝒊𝒕𝒉 𝒂 𝑯𝒂𝒓𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒔, 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒔𝒕𝒐𝒑 𝒃𝒖𝒊𝒍𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒑𝒍𝒖𝒎𝒃𝒊𝒏𝒈. 𝒀𝒐𝒖 𝒋𝒖𝒔𝒕 𝒂𝒅𝒅 𝒚𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒄𝒖𝒔𝒕𝒐𝒎 𝒕𝒐𝒐𝒍𝒔 (𝒌𝒖𝒃𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒍, 𝑨𝑷𝑰𝒔, 𝒅𝒂𝒕𝒂𝒃𝒂𝒔𝒆𝒔) 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒄𝒖𝒔𝒕𝒐𝒎𝒊𝒛𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒔𝒚𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒎 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒎𝒑𝒕. The Shift: - With a 𝐅𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤, you spend time building the infrastructure. - With a 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬, you start with a functional runtime on Day 1. Great conversation with Sam Partee (Arcade.dev) and Harrison Chase (LangChain) on the AI-native infrastructure revolution. Key insights: 1. Models are finally reliable enough to run in loops and call tools autonomously 2. AI-native infrastructure is fundamentally different from cloud-native – it requires new patterns for observability, security, and tool composition 3. The biggest blocker? Application quality. Better context engineering and observability are critical. 4. Security model shift: Assume agents have the same permissions as whoever they're exposed to (prompt injection is real) The "plumbing" layer for agents is being built right now – MCP, sandboxes, audit logs, and proper auth pass-through are becoming table stakes. We're witnessing a generational shift in how software gets built. Not replacing cloud-native, but layering on top with entirely new requirements.
